IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL  NO.         OF 2026
(@ SLP(C) No.25843/2026)
RAJESH K. MEHTA                                    APPELLANT(s)
                                VERSUS
HDFC BANK LIMITED                                  RESPONDENT(S)
WITH
CIVIL APPEAL  NO.         OF 2026
(@SLP(C) No(s).28456/2026)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Two sets of appeals are placed before us for consideration.
Civil Appeal @ SLP (C) 25843/2026 is filed by the appellant –
Rajesh K. Mehta, aggrieved over the condition imposed by the
High Court, while granting permission to travel abroad and
Civil Appeal @ SLP (C) 28456/2026 has been filed by the
appellant-Lilavati Kirtilal Mehta Medical Trust (for short,
‘the Trust’) after seeking leave, since the said appellant was
not a party before the High Court.
3. These appeals before us lie on a very narrow compass. 
4. By way of the impugned order dated 16.07.2026 passed by the
High Court of Judicature at Bombay, the High Court granted
permission to the appellant-Rajesh K. Mehta, to travel abroad

--- Page 82 ---
2
for a period of 120 days, subject to certain conditions,
including  a  monetary  condition  of  depositing  a  sum  of
Rs.7,50,00,000/- (Rupees seven crores and fifty lakhs) as an
additional security.
5. Dr. Abhishek Manu Singhvi, learned Senior counsel and Mr.
Devdatt  Kamat,  learned  Senior  counsel  appearing  for  the
appellant – Rajesh K. Mehta submit that the Recovery Officer,
Debts Recovery Tribunal (for short, ‘DRT’) No. II, Mumbai,
himself has modified the earlier order dated 25.10.2023, by
withdrawing the arrest warrant vide order dated 22.07.2025 and
all  other  travel  restrictions  imposed  on  the  appellant.
Therefore, in law, there is no bar. The reason why the
appellant has filed the interim application before the High
Court to travel abroad, was due to the reason that the
respondent - HDFC Bank, by placing reliance upon the previous
order,  had  raised  an  objection  before  the  Immigration
Authorities. The said situation no longer prevails. The mere
fact that the order enuring to the benefit of the appellant
has been challenged and is pending consideration in a writ
petition, cannot be a ground to impose the condition of
depositing  a  sum  of  Rs.7,50,00,000/-  as  an  additional
security. 
6. The appellant has already shown his bonafides in the past by
returning to India, after making frequent visits abroad. His
family resides in Belgium and he has already previously
deposited a sum of Rs.7,50,00,000/- and, in fact, a total sum

--- Page 83 ---
3
of Rs.12 Crores has been deposited or paid so far. All the
properties of the appellant have been secured and the other
conditions imposed by the High Court in the impugned order,
would be sufficient. 
7. In such view of the matter, the condition imposed to deposit
an additional security amount will have to be set aside,
particularly, when there are no criminal proceedings pending
against the appellant – Rajesh K. Mehta. 
8. The learned Senior counsel appearing for the respondent – Bank
would submit that it is a case where the appellant - Rajesh K.
Mehta has not placed the correct facts before this Court.
Therefore, there is no need to entertain the present appeal
seeking grant of the relief sought for. The High Court did
take into consideration the equities, and has passed the
impugned order. It is not factually correct to state that the
properties are available for sale and have been encumbered in
one way or other. Considering the facts governing, especially,
the pendency of the Writ Petition No.3802/2025 challenging the
order(s) passed by the Recovery Officer, DRT-II, Mumbai, there
is  no  need  for  interference  with  the  impugned  order.
Additionally, it is prayed that taking note of the facts, the
very order passed by the High Court will have to be set aside.
9. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the parties
and perused the records.  
10. It is not in dispute that the appellant did make frequent
travels abroad and returned back to India. He is also not a

--- Page 84 ---
4
flight risk. These two factors, in fact, have been taken note
of by the High Court itself. Additionally, we find that, as on
today, the order of the Recovery Officer, DRT-II, Mumbai dated
22.07.2025 enures to the benefit of the appellant-Rajesh K.
Mehta. 
11. In such view of the matter, there is no bar for the appellant-
Rajesh K. Mehta to travel abroad. However, the High Court has
exercised its discretion by imposing the condition to deposit
an additional sum as security. 
12. In such view of the matter, the only issue for consideration
is whether the said condition imposed by the High Court is
just and proper, since we do not find any merit in the appeal
filed by the Trust, challenging the very permission granted in
favour of the appellant to travel abroad. 
13. It is the submission of the learned Senior counsel appearing
for the appellant-Rajesh K. Mehta that all the properties
belonging to the appellant have been attached and he is not in
a position to comply with the monetary condition imposed vide
the impugned order. While the learned Senior counsel appearing
for the respondent-Bank, by placing reliance upon one of the
orders passed by the High Court, would submit that a factual
finding has been recorded by the Recovery Officer, DRT-II,
Mumbai himself that the appellant has got sufficient financial
means. 
14. Taking note of the aforesaid position, we are only inclined to
modify the condition imposed by the High Court by reducing the

--- Page 85 ---
5
sum of Rs.7,50,00,000/- to a sum of Rs.3,00,00,000/- (Rupees
Three Crores). The appellant-Rajesh K. Mehta is directed to
deposit the modified security amount in the same manner, as
directed by the High Court. The aforesaid compliance will have
to be made within a period of three days before undertaking
the proposed travel. 
15. We make it clear that within the time if the appellant comes
back, the same cannot be construed as the complete compliance
of the order, as the ultimate outer limit granted by the High
Court was of 120 days, which enables him to undertake further
travel within the same. 
16. To put an end to the lis in one way or the other, we request
the High Court to make an endeavour to dispose of pending writ
petitions  bearing  W.P.  No.3802/2025  and  W.P.  (L)
No.40817/2025, within a period of six months from the date of
receipt of a copy of this order.  
17. The Presiding Officer, DRT-II, Mumbai is also directed to
dispose of the pending matter being M.A. No.119/2025 in R.P.
No.709/2004, within a period six months from the date of
receipt of a copy of this order.  
18. By way of a clarification, we make it clear that all the
pending proceedings will have to be decided on their own
merits, without being influenced by the observations made in
the impugned order.

--- Page 86 ---
6
19. Both the appeals are disposed of in the aforesaid terms.
20. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. A note has been submitted by learned Senior Counsel
Mr. M. L. Lahoty for the home buyers informing this Court
that the Forensic Auditors appointed by this Court have
submitted a detailed Report in eight Volumes furnishing
all minute details of siphoning of Rs.5619.47 Crores from
home buyers.
2. He has stated that only Rs.744.81 Crores have been
recovered  so  far.  The  major  chunk  of  recovery  of
Rs.2159.32  Crores  is  due  from  Promoters/Directors  as
recorded in the main judgment at page Nos.331, 332, 336
and 337.
3. He has further stated that an amount of Rs.760.05
13

--- Page 110 ---
Crores has to be recovered from Surekha Family and an
amount of Rs.100 Crores has to be recovered from one
Mr. Prem Mishra. It has also been brought to the notice of
this Court that approximately Rs.2159.32 Crores have to
recovered  from  Promoters/Directors/CFOs  etc.,  however,
nothing has been recovered from them so far. In addition
to the aforesaid recovery of Rs.386.55 crores is to be
made from various third party entities. The Enforcement
Directorate (hereinafter referred to as “ED”)  has filed a
report in the matter but unfortunately details have not
been furnished in respect of the recoveries made/action
taken by the ED against Directors/Promoters/CFOs.
4. The ED is, therefore, directed to take immediate
action  against  the  Promoters/Directors/CFOs  etc.  for
recovering the amount which has been quantified in the
Forensic Auditos Report. The ED shall treat this matter at
top priority as fraud has been committed upon as many as
46,000 home buyers and inspite of judgment delivered by
this Court in the year 2019 and out of Rs.5619.47 Crores
only Rs.744.81 Crores have been recovered, so far.
5. Learned ASG has fairly stated before this Court that
the ED will certainly take immediate steps for recovery of
the money, however, she has stated that cases are pending
before various PMLA Courts and a direction should be
issued to the PMLA Courts to conclude/decide the cases as
expeditiously as possible.
14

--- Page 111 ---
6. Learned  ASG  has  furnished  details  of  certain
properties in the affidavit, however, the affidavit does
not  disclose  all  the  properties  which  are  allegedly
proceeds of crime and the action taken in respect of those
properties. Resultantly, time is granted to the ED to file
a Status Report after three weeks and the Status Report
shall furnish all minute details in respect of the further
action proposed to be taken by the ED keeping in view the
judgment delivered by this Court in the matter and the
directions issued from time to time.
7. It is the duty of the ED to ensure recovery of the
siphoned off amount proceeds of crime as expeditiously as
possible  at  an  early  date  by  following  the  process
prescribed under the law.
8. The  Appellate  Tribunals  shall  also  decide  the
matters pending before all the Appellate Tribunals as
expeditiously as possible.
9. List on 26.10.2026 at 2:00 pm.

withdraw I.A. Nos.279582/2026 and 279591/2026. Permission
is granted. Said applications are dismissed as withdrawn.

     O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Challenge in these appeals is to the
order(s) passed by the Division Bench of the

--- Page 127 ---
2
High Court disposing of the Writ Petition(s)
preferred by the respondents, wherein challenge
was laid to the amendment incorporated in Rule
6(9)  of  the  Odisha  Civil  Services
(Rehabilitation  Assistance)  Rules,  2020
(hereinafter  referred  to  as  ‘the  Rules  of
2020’).
3. To be precise, Odisha Civil Services
(Rehabilitation  Assistance)  Rules,  1990
(hereinafter referred to as ‘Rules of 1990’)
were substituted by a  new set of Rules namely,
Rules of 2020. Sub Rule 9 of Rule 6 thereof,
provided that all pending cases as on the date
of publication of these Rules in the Odisha
Gazette, shall be dealt in accordance with the
provisions of these Rules.
4. The Writ Petitioners before the High
Court,  were  aggrieved  by  this  clause  as,
according to them, they were meted with less
beneficial or inferior treatment under Rules of
2020 in comparison to the Rules prevailing at
the time of death of the employee(s).
5. The High Court, under the impugned
order,  observed that Rule 6(9) of the Rules of

--- Page 128 ---
3
2020 takes away Writ Petitioners’ right to be
considered under the old Rules and therefore,
the same is arbitrary.
6. In  consequence,  the  High  Court
issued the following directions, as contained in
paragraph nos. 84,85 and 86 of the impugned
order, which are reproduced hereunder for ready
reference;
“84. In view of the above decision, we
are of the view that the application for the
petitioners shall be considered under the
Odisha  Civil  Services  (Rehabilitation
Assistance) Rules, 1990 in as much as on
scrutiny,  it  is  found  that  all  the
applications were filed before 17.02.2020
and  the  delay  in  considering  the
applications  in  time  is  entirely
attributable to the opposite parties. Such
exercise shall be completed within a period
of three months from the day when a copy of
the judgment/order shall be placed before
the opposite parties by the petitioners.
85.  That  apart,  while  dealing  with  the
applications in which the petitioners have
sought  the  rehabilitation
assistance/appointment  against  a  direct
payment/GIA Rules at the Government aided
educational institution, the applicability
of  the  rehabilitation  scheme  in  those
institutions shall be separately determined
by the opposite parties on the basis of the
policy of the Government as discussed by us.
If  it  is  found  that  the  Odisha  Civil
Services (Rehabilitation Assistance) Rules,
1990 was applicable on the date of death of

--- Page 129 ---
4
the deceased employee, the petitioner shall
be  considered  for  rehabilitation
assistance/appointment.  So  far  as  the
retrospective  operation  of  the
rehabilitation  assistance/appointment  is
concerned,  this  Court  cannot  direct  the
opposite parties to give the appointment
retrospectively  under  the  Rehabilitation
Assistance/ Appointment Scheme in as much as
it is no more res integra, the petitioner
does  not  have  any  vested  right  of
appointment  under  such  rehabilitation
assistance/appointment scheme. They are only
entitled to be considered under the scheme
for that purpose.
86. Consequently, the opposite parties shall
consider the applications of the petitioners
under  the  Odisha  Civil  Services
(Rehabilitation Assistance) Rules, 1990 read
with  the  relevant  policy  extending  such
scheme to the Government aided educational
institutions at the relevant time of the
death  of  the  deceased  employee  for  the
purpose  of  the  rehabilitation
assistance/appointment within the time as
prescribed above.”
7.  Mr.  Pitambar  Acharya,  learned
Advocate General appearing for the appellant-
State  of  Odisha  would  place  before  us  an
Amendment published in the Odisha Gazette dated
04  April,  2025  named  Odisha  Civil  Services
(Rehabilitation  Assistance)  Rules,  2025
(hereinafter referred to as ‘Rules of 2025’. In
this amendment, Sub Rule 9 of Rule 6 has been

--- Page 130 ---
5
substituted in the following manner;
“ (i) for sub-rule (9), the following sub-
rule shall be substituted, namely:-
"(9)  (a)   All  pending  applications,
relating to death of Government employee
prior to the date of commencement of the
Odisha  Civil  Services  (Rehabilitation
Assistance) Rules, 2020 shall be dealt in
accordance with the rules prevailing on the
date of death of Government employee for
appointment under Rehabilitation Assistance
Scheme:
Provided that in case the death of
Government employee occurred on or after
commencement of the Odisha Civil Service
(Rehabilitation  Assistance)  Amendment
Rules, 2016 and before commencement of the
Odisha  Civil  Services  (Rehabilitation
Assistance)Rules, 2020, shall be governed
by  the  provisions  of  the  Odisha  Civil
Service  (Rehabilitation  Assistance)
Rules,1990.
(b) In  case  the  death  of  Government
employee occurred prior to commencement of
the Odisha Civil Service (Rehabilitation
Assistance) Amendment Rules, 2016, shall be
dealt on the basis of distress certificate
available  in  the  existing  or  original
application as per the Odisha Civil Service
(Rehabilitation Assistance) Rules,
(c) In  case  the  death  of  Government
employee occurred on or after commencement
of the Odisha Civil Service (Rehabilitation
Assistance)  Amendment  Rules,  2016  and
before commencement of the Odisha Civil
Services (Rehabilitation Assistance) Rules,
2020,  the  appointing  authority  shall
ascertain the present financial distress of

--- Page 131 ---
6
the family by  calling for a report from
Collector of the district in which the
family ordinarily resides, as to whether
the family is in financial distress as per
the provisions of rule 8 of the Odisha
Civil Service (Rehabilitation Assistance)
Rules, 1990.
Explanation  for  the  distress
certificate prescribed under clause (c)-
The total annual family income from
all sources excluding Family pension and
temporary  increase  must  not  exceed
Rs.1,91,000/-(Rupees One Lakh and Ninety-
One Thousand) for a family to be in a
distress condition'."
8. Learned  Advocate  General,  Mr.
Pitambar Acharya, for the State would submit
that basis 2025 amendment, as extracted above,
the  challenge  to  the  first  part  of  the
directions issued by the High Court would not
survive.  Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
respondents would not dispute this position as
after the said amendment or, under the impugned
order passed by the High Court, respondents
would be covered under the Rules which were
prevailing immediately prior to the enactment of
Rules of 2020.
9. In view of the above, the first part
of the challenge so as to the applicability of

--- Page 132 ---
7
Rules of 1990, would not survive and the same
shall be governed under the 2025 amendment.
10. We  are  now  left  with  second
limb of challenge to the impugned order, wherein
the High Court has directed consideration and
applicability of Rules of 2020, as amended in
the year 2025, to the employees of Government
Aided  Educational  Institution.  According  to
learned  Advocate  General,  the  directions
contained in paragraph nos. 85 and 86 of the
impugned order, may be treated as being applied
also on ‘block grant’ employees where as, the
issue is yet to be resolved at the Government
level by taking an appropriate duly considered
policy decision.
11. In  our  view,  even  the  High
Court has not issued any Writ directing the
State Government to cover the ‘block grant’
employees  in  the  compassionate  apointment
scheme. What the High Court has directed the
State Government is that whether or not the
employees  of  Government  Aided  educational
institutions  are  entitled  for  consideration,
will be determined on the basis of the extant

--- Page 133 ---
8
policy of the Government on the date of death of
such employees. The High Court has also directed
consideration of the respondents’ application(s)
under the Rules of 1990 read with the relevant
policy extending such scheme to the Government
aided educational institution at the time of the
death  of  the  deceased  employee(s)  for  the
purpose  of  rehabilitation  assistance/
appointment within the time as prescribed above.
12. Thus, whether or not, a ‘block
grant employee’, who is yet to become a part of
the Government Aided Educational Institutions
having received 100% aid, shall be decided by
the  State  Government,  as  submitted  by  the
learned Advocate General, Mr. Pitambar Acharya,
appearing for the appellant-State of Odisha. We
expect  the  State  Government  to  take  the
decision, as indicated above, within a period of
six months from today.
13. In view of the above, in our
considered view, there is no occasion for us to
adjudicate on both the directions issued by the
High Court.

--- Page 134 ---
9
14. Accordingly,  the  appeals  are
disposed of with the above observations.
15. Pending application(s), if any,
shall stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Our order dated 13th November, 2025 is relevant for the purpose
of the order that we propose to pass today.
2. Our order dated 13th November, 2025 reads thus:-
“1. We heard Mr. R Venkataramani, the learned Attorney General for
India appearing for the Union of India, Mr. Gaurav Sharma, the
learned  senior  counsel  appearing  for  the  National  Medical
Commission of India and Mr. Sanjay R. Hegde, the learned counsel
appearing for some of the students.
2. We are happy to note that there is some substantial progress in
the matter for which we are very grateful to the learned Attorney
General. 
3. In a meeting which was convened between all stakeholders
excluding the College of Physician and Surgeon, in principle the
authorities have reached to the following understanding:-
“a. Students may be categorized as follows: 
1. CATEGORY -1: Students enrolled in any of the 10 
qualifications (i.e. 6 FCPS course, 3 Diploma Course and 1 MCPS 
course) up to the academic year 2022-2023; 
ii. CATEGORY-II: Students enrolled in any of the 10 
qualifications (Le. 6 FCPS course, 3 Diploma Course and 1 MCPS 
course) in academic year 2023-2024 and onwards; 
iii. CATEGORY-III: Student enrolled in courses other than the 
above mentioned 10 qualifications in academic year 2017-2018, 
2018-2019 etc. 
b. Regarding Category-1, Ministry of Health & Family Welfare
(MoHFW) in consultation with National Medical Commission (NMC),
after due deliberation and discussion with all bodies involved
in conducting of examination, with a view to protect the
interest of the students, and as a one-time measure, has decided
5

--- Page 176 ---
as under: 
i. Category I students whose final examinations are due shall be
permitted  to  appear  in  their  final  examination  of  their
respective FCPS/Diploma/MCPS course.
ii. As a onetime measure, the examination shall be conducted by
the CPS in a fair and transparent manner, as per their course
curriculum, not later 3 months from the date allowed by this
Hon'ble Court. 
iii. Students shall be granted only 2 attempts to pass the
examination. 2nd attempt, if any, to be conducted within a
period of 2 months after the declaration of results of 1st
examination.  No  additional  attempts  will  be  given  to  the
students for appearing in the examination. 
iv.  Students  successfully  passing  the  examination  will  be
entitled to have the qualification FCPS/Diplomat MCPS as granted
by CPS entered in the State Medical Council / National Medical
Commission, as the case may be. Students will not be entitled to
claim any additional benefit or privilege, except having FCPS/
Diploma/ MCPS entered in State Medical Register / National
Medical Register. 
c. For this category of students it is further suggested that: 
i. Permission may be granted to appear in the final examinations
of respective FCPS/Diploma/MCPS courses
ii. Examination to be conducted by CPS, as a one-time measure,
within 3 months.
iii. Only two attempts allowed; second attempt within 2 months
of first result.
iv. Successful candidates' qualifications to be entered in
state/National Medical Registers. 
d. For Category II, as per the list furnished by CPS there are
239 students. These students have been admitted by CPS despite
MoHFW letter dated 19.07.2024, wherein, MoHFW has made it
unequivocally clear that no admission can be granted by CPS for
the a.y. 2023-2024. By the said letter, CPS was categorically
informed by MoHFW the last date for admission as fixed by this
Hon'ble Court is already over. Despite there being specific
direction  from  MoHFW,  CPS  has  deliberately  admitted  these
students. It is also pertinent to mention that by this time
PGMEB,  NMC  had  de-  recognized  /  discontinued  the  courses
conducted  by  CPS.  The  admission  are  completely  illegal.
Extension of the length being given to Category 1, to this
6

--- Page 177 ---
Category will be a matter of consideration for this Hon'ble
Court. 
e. In this category, as per the list furnished by CPS, CPS has
included many admissions in different qualifications (other than
the above 10 qualifications) from 2017 onwards. On an earlier
occasion, MoHFW vide its letter dated 18.10.2022 had regularized
the qualification granted to 466 students by CPS who were
admitted between 17.1.2017 to 22.01.2018. CPS has not explained
as to how the names of these students did not figure earlier and
has now cropped up for the 1st time after 7 years. CPS in its
list has added students who have failed the course in the year
2017 and 2018. It appears that the attempt of CPS is to procure
additional attempts for every student who has been enrolled in
the past. Extension of the length being given to Category I, to
this Category will be a matter of consideration for this Hon'ble
Court.”
4. It appears that there are almost 852 students in Category (I).
So far as the Category (II) is concerned, there are around 239
students and insofar as the Category (III) is concerned, there are
57 students.
5. Insofar as all those students falling in Category (I) are
concerned, their interest has been well protected. Insofar as the
students falling in Category (II) is concerned, we take notice of
the fact that the CPS had admitted them despite letter received
from MoHFW dated 19.7.2024 informing that no admission should be
granted  for  AY  2023-2024,  the  students  were  admitted.  The
respondents are not inclined to afford any protection to the
students falling in Category (II). Insofar as the students falling
in Category (III) are concerned, they are around 57 in numbers.
They have already completed their entire course long time back. 
6. Today, we may only request the learned Attorney General and Mr.
Gaurav Sharma to once again re-consider the decision insofar the
as Category (III) is concerned.
7.  We  enquired  with  the  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
petitioner(s) as to who are the students, who are falling in each
of the categories. However, they do not have the necessary data in
this regard. In such circumstances, the CPS shall provide a
complete correct & statement of all the students with their names
falling in three different categories i.e. Category No.I, Category
7

--- Page 178 ---
No.II  and  Category  No.III  respectively  by  the  next  date  of
hearing. 
8. List on 18.12.2025. 
9. Once the entire list of the students is placed before us, we
shall thereafter proceed to pass an order to publish it and make
it public. 
10.  We  once  again  request  the  Learned  Attorney  General  to
reconsider students falling within Category III.”
3. Thus, by our order dated 13th November, 2025 referred to above,
we had classified the students in three categories. We have
recorded in our order dated 13th November, 2025 that the interest of
all the students falling in Category (I) has been well protected.
4. We have also recorded that insofar as the students falling in
Category (II) are concerned, the CPS had admitted them despite
letter received from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
(MoHFW) informing that no admission be granted for A.Y. 2023-2024.
5. Insofar  as  the  students  falling  in  Category  (III)  are
concerned, the have already completed their entire course long time
back.
6. Today, we propose to take care of all those students who are
falling in Category (IV).
7. We are informed that there are, in all, 962 students falling
in Category (IV). It is not in dispute that they have also
completed their course. All that is now left is the examination.
8. Insofar as the challenge to the impugned judgment and order
passed by the High Court is concerned, we will be hearing all the
learned counsel. We shall decide the legality and validity of the
impugned judgment and order on its own merits, however, we firmly
8

--- Page 179 ---
believe that let the students be relieved of this entire imbroglio
that has been created.
9. In such circumstances, we direct that let 962 students of the
IVth Category, shall be permitted to appear in the examination as
may be scheduled by the authority concerned. Let the authority
proceed to fix the program of the examination and inform each and
every student to prepare themselves.
10. How to schedule the examination, is for the authority to plan
it out. It is needless to clarify that the examinations shall be
for all the four categories of students.
11. We further make it clear that there shall not be any fresh
admission of students in the petitioner college/course till we
pronounce the final judgment.
12. We make it clear that these 962 students falling in Category
(IV) shall be permitted to appear in the examination despite there
being any objection at the end of the National Medical Commission
(NMC) and the Union of India.
13. In the peculiar facts and circumstance of this case, we have
passed this order.
14. The main matter shall now be notified for final hearing on
23rd September, 2026.
(HARPREET KAUR)                                 (POOJA SHARMA)
COURT MASTER (SH)                             COURT MASTER (NSH)

O R D E R 
DIPANKAR DATTA, J. 
1. The present batch of civil appeals and special leave petitions1 assail the common 
judgment and order of the High Court for the State of Telangana at Hyderabad 2 
dated 27th December, 2023 in Writ Petition Nos. 18002, 188 42 and 18880 of 
2023 as well as the common judgment and order of the High Court dated 2nd 
May, 2024 in Writ Petition Nos. 12527 and 12289 of 2024. Relying on the order 
dated 2nd May, 2024, one more writ petition, i.e., Writ Petition No. 12886 of 2024, 
was decided by the High Court on 3rd May, 2024 which has also been challenged 
before us.  
2. There is also a connected writ petition before us [W.P. (C) No. 489/2024], which 
has been presented seeking the relief of quashing the criteri on for eligibility  in 
the Telangana State Judicial Service Rules, 2023 3, Notification No. 87/2024-RC 
dated 10 th April, 2024 and Notification No. R.O.C. No. 87/2024 -RC dated 24 th 
July, 2024, precluding the writ petitioners from appearing in the recruitment 
examination (written) in absence of certificate of enrolment from  a Bar 
Association in the Telangana State. Direction was sought to  the State and the 
High Court to permit the writ petitioners to appear in the Written Examination 
 
1 SLPs 
2 High Court  
3 2023 Rules 

--- Page 199 ---
3 
 
(Mains) for the post of Civil Judge (Junior Division) in the State Judicial Service 
even in  the absence of the requisite  certificate of being enrolled with a Bar 
Association in Telangana.  
3. There were also intervention applications [IA No. 173072/2024, IA No. 
169060/2024, IA No. 173271/2024 and IA No. 173128/2024 in SLP(C) No. 
11655/2024], which have been  filed seeking to implead certain writ petitioners 
before the High Court as co -petitioners. Such applications were allowed by the 
learned Chamber Judge vide order dated 30 th September, 2024. Office Report 
dated 20th August, 2025 notes that upon such order, the applicants were made 
co-petitioners and the cause title has been amended.  
4. The material facts are noted from the present appeals. These facts are indicative 
of all the matters before us. Briefly put, the facts are these: 
a. The State of Telangana 4 issued G.O. Ms. No . 59 dated 15 th July, 2017  
framing the Telangana State Judicial (Service and Cadre) Rules, 20175. On 
6th January, 2020 , the State issued G. O. Ms. No. 31 effecting certain 
amendments to the 2017 Rules.  
b. On 12th April 2023, the State issued Notification No. 180/2023-Rc inviting 
applications for appointment on 11 (eleven) posts of District Judge (Entry 
Level) by direct recruitment in the Telangana State Judicial Service. This 
notification posited that advocates practicing in the High Court or Courts 
 
4 State 
5 2017 Rules 

--- Page 200 ---
4 
 
working under the control of the High Court for 7 years would be eligible to 
apply.  
c. Appellants/petitioners and others, perceiving that they possessed the 
requisite qualifications, offered their candidature by submitting applications 
in April 2023 for participating in the recruitment process.  
d. The State issued Notification vide G.O. Ms. No. 36 dated 10th June, 2023, 
whereby special rules in the form of the 2023 Rules  were introduced in 
supersession of the extant rules. Rule 5 (5.1) (a) of the 2023 Rules read as 
follows:  
5. Eligibility for Direct Recruitment and Recruitment by transfer:  
(5.1) District Judges (Entry Level) Direct Recruitment:  
A person to be appointed to the category of District Judge by direct 
recruitment shall be:  
(a) One who has been practicing as an Advocate in the High Court or 
Courts working under the control of the High Court for not less than 
7 years as on the date of the notification.  
Provided that a full time salaried Law Officer in the Employment of 
the Central Government or State Government or any Public 
Corporation or Body constituted by statute shall not be eligible for 
the post of District Judge.  
…  
Rule 2(k) of the 2023 Rules reads as follows:  
2. Definitions: In these Rules unless the context otherwise requires:- 
… 
(k) “High Court” means and includes High Court for the State of 
Telangana w.e.f. 02.06.2014; 
… 
e. The Registrar of the High Court issued a list vide Notification dated 3rd July, 
2023. It contained a list of applicants who were rejected . 

--- Page 201 ---
5 
 
Appellants/petitioners figured in such list. The common reason for rejection 
of their candidature was that they were not eligible to participate in the 
recruitment process in terms of Rule 5(1)(a)  [sic. Rule 5(5.1)(a)]  of the 
2023 Rules.  
f. Thoroughly dissatisfied with such rejection, the appellants /petitioners 
invoked the writ jurisdiction of the High Court by presenting petitions under 
Article 226 of the Constitution of India6.  
g. By an order dated 12 th July, 2023 passed on W.P. No. 18002 of 2023, the 
High Court granted interim relief permitting the appellants/petitioners to 
appear in the written examination scheduled to be held on 22nd July, 2023 
and 23rd July, 2023.  
h. Appellants/petitioners participated in the written examination and claim to 
have secured qualifying marks.  
i. An Official Memorandum  dated 16 th October, 2023  was sent by the 
Registrar of the High Court to the appellants/petitioners with a request to 
appear for the oral interview (viva-voce).  
j. The Registrar of the High Court filed a counter affidavit in W.P. No. 18880 
of 2023 in November, 2023.  
 
6 Constitution 

--- Page 202 ---
6 
 
k. Vide the impugned common judgment and final order dated 27th December, 
2023, the writ petitions filed by the appellants/petitioners were dismissed 
on the ground that: 
i. The 2023 Rules are not in contravention of Article 233 of the 
Constitution;  
ii. The 2023 Rules  came to be enacted on 10 th June, 2023 with 
retrospective effect from 01st January, 2023;  
iii. ‘High Court’ as mentioned in Rule 2(k) of the 2023 Rules does not 
include other High Courts and refers only to the High Court of 
Telangana; and 
iv. Since the appellants/petitioners are not practicing advocates in the 
High Court, they did not have the requisite seven years of experience 
and, therefore, could not contend that Rule 5(1)(a) [sic Rule 
5(5.1)(a)] of the 2023 Rules was discriminatory, arbitrary, and 
violative of Article 14 of the Constitution.   
5. Before we part with the facts, one other aspect  is this . Those aspiring for 
appointment as Civil Judge (Junior Division) have approached this Court b y 
presenting W.P. (C) No. 489 of 2024, as noted above. This Court by order dated 
6th August, 2024, while issuing notice, permitted the writ petitioners to participate 
in the recruitment process initiated by the High Court by its notification dated 
10th April, 2024, subject to such further orders as may be passed in these 
proceedings. However, the result of these writ petitioners were not to be declared 
pending further orders of this Court.  

--- Page 203 ---
7 
 
6. Learned senior counsel for the appellants, learned counsel for the petitioners in 
the SLPs, learned counsel for the writ petitioner, learned counsel for the 
intervenors, learned senior c ounsel for the High Court and learned counsel for 
the State were heard at some length. Multiple decisions were cited at the bar on 
either side. We had the occasion to peruse the same.  
7. Looking at the said decisions and w hile reserving judgment on these 
appeals/SLPs/writ petition, learned senior counsel  representing the High Court 
was requested by us to seek instructions on certain alternatives that were 
suggested with the rider that acceptance of the suggestion favourable to the 
appellants/petitioners/intervenors/writ petitioners  would not be treated as a 
precedent.  
8. Additional/Supplementary submissions on the behalf of the High Court  having 
been filed in the Registry of this Court on 28 th August, 2025, the same were 
subsequently circulated to us. The submissions note that after judgment was 
reserved, learned senior counsel apprised the High Court on the alternatives 
suggested. It is further revealed therefrom that the High Court has no objection 
to declare the results and to appoint such of the 
appellants/petitioners/intervenors who have qualified the 2023 recruitment 
examination for appointment as District Judges as an exceptional case without 
unsettling the 2023 Rules.   
9. We appreciate the stand taken by the High Court and, accordingly, request the 
High Court to declare the results of the appellants/petitioners/intervenors and to 
proceed for verification of their credentials/antecedents. Such of the qualified 

--- Page 204 ---
8 
 
appellants/petitioners/intervenors who are found suitable may be appointed  by 
offering them letters of appointment, as a special case, as early as possible but 
not later than two months from date of service of a copy of this order on the High 
Court. Needless to observe, this order is strictly confined to the facts and 
circumstances of the appeals and petitions before us and may not be treated as 
a precedent for future cases. It is also clarified that since the appointments are 
being offered acceding to a suggestion of this Court, the 
appellants/petitioners/intervenors, upon their appointment as District Judge shall 
not be entitled to claim any arrears of monetary benefits and their seniority shall 
be determined based on their dates of appointment, meaning thereby that those 
who have already been appointed shall rank senior to them.  
10. There shall be similar directi on for the writ petitioners who participated in the 
examination pursuant to the order dated 6th August, 2024. 
11. Needless to observe, all question(s) of law raised before us is/are kept open.   
12. The civil appeals, the SLPs and the writ petition are disposed of on the above 
terms. Parties shall, however, bear their own costs.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.         OF 2026
(@ SLP(CRL.) NO. 11631/2026)
PRANALI KARAN PATIL & ANR.               Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
THE STATE OF MAHARASHTRA & ANR.         Respondent(s)
 O R D E R
Leave granted.
This appeal challenges the order dated 11.06.2026
passed by the High Court of Judicature at Bombay in
Anticipatory Bail Application No. 959/2026.
Apprehending  arrest  in  connection  with  crime
registered pursuant to FIR No.594 of 2023 lodged with
Hinjewadi Police Station, Pimpri Chinchwad District in
respect of the offences punishable under Sections 420,
404, 406, 381, 468, 471 and 120(B) of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860 (in short, “IPC”), the appellants preferred
an  application(s)  before  the  High  Court  seeking
anticipatory bail in terms of Section 438 of the Code
of Criminal Procedure, 1973 [in short, “the Code”]. 

--- Page 206 ---
2
Said application(s) for anticipatory bail has been
rejected by the High Court vide the impugned order
dated  11.06.2026.  Hence,  instant  appeal  has  been
preferred.
By order dated 24.06.2026, this Court has passed
the following order:
“1. Issue notice to the respondents, returnable on
14.08.2026. 
2. Learned standing counsel, Mr. Aaditya Aniruddha
Pande accepts notice for the respondent-State.
3.  Learned  Advocate-on-Record,  Mr.  Jaydip  Pati
accepts notice for second respondent/caveator.
4. Till the next date of hearing, no coercive steps
shall be taken as against the petitioners herein
vis-a-vis  FIR  No.594/2023  dated  07.05.2023
registered at Police Station Hinjewadi, District
Pimri-Chinchwad,  Maharashtra  subject  to  the
petitioners cooperating with the investigation.”
We have heard learned senior counsel in support
of  the  appellants  and  learned  counsel  for  the
respondent-State  and  learned  senior  counsel  for
respondent No.2.
Learned  senior  counsel  for  the  appellants
submitted that pursuant to the interim order dated
24.06.2026, the appellants have been cooperating with

--- Page 207 ---
3
the  investigation  which  is  still  continuing.  He
further submitted that appellant No.1 is nursing a
sixteen months’ infant whereas appellant No.2 is her
brother and brother-in-law of the main accused. He
contended  that  having  regard  to  the  fact  that
respondent No.2 has already filed a suit seeking a
declaration that the testament on which the appellants
are relying is illegal and the suit is at large
between  the  parties,  at  this  stage  refusal  of
anticipatory bail to the appellants herein may be a
travesty of justice. He, therefore, contended that the
interim order may be made absolute subject to the
conditions to be imposed by this Court. 
Per contra, learned counsel appearing for the
first respondent-State with reference to his Statement
of Objections contended that no doubt the appellants
are cooperating with the investigation which is still
on and however the fact remains that the appellants
herein have been contumacious in the fabrication of a
Will.  Therefore  the  invocation  of  the  various
provisions have been justifiable made. He submitted
that there is no merit in this appeal. 

--- Page 208 ---
4
Learned senior counsel appearing for respondent
No. 2 also contended that there is no merit in this
appeal and submitted that the appellants herein have
misused their proximity to the deceased-testator and
hence, the relief of anticipatory bail may not be
granted to them.
Considering the circumstances on record, in our
view,  the  appellants  are  entitled  to  the  relief
claimed under Section 438 of the Code.
We, therefore, allow this appeal and set aside
the order passed by the High Court dated 11.06.2026.
We  direct  that  in  the  event  of  arrest  of  the
appellants, the Arresting Officer shall release the
appellants on bail subject to furnishing cash security
in the sum of Rs.25,000/- (Rupees Twenty-Five Thousand
only) with two like sureties.
It is directed that the appellants shall extend
complete cooperation in the ensuing investigation. The
appellants shall not misuse their liberty and shall
not in any way influence the witnesses or tamper with
the material on record.

--- Page 209 ---
5
With  the  aforesaid  directions,  the  Criminal
Appeal is allowed.

1. Leave granted.
2. These appeals, at the instance of the appellants/secured
creditors, arise out of a common judgment and order dated 3 rd June,
20251 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court of Judicature at
Madras, Madurai Bench whereby the Division Bench allowed several
writ petitions2 filed by the respective respondents/borrowers. While
setting aside sale notices issued pursuant to measures taken in
terms of the provisions contained in Section 13 of the Securitisation
and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security
Interest Act, 2002 3 and the rules framed thereunder, the Division
Bench also observed that since the borrowers were Micro Small and
Medium Enterprises 4, the secured creditors ought to formulate a
revival and rehabilitation scheme in terms of notification dated 29 th
May, 2015 issued by the Joint Secretary to the Government of India,
Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. 
3. In course of pendency of these proceedings, opportunity was
extended to all the borrowers to offer terms of settlement to the
secured creditors. Final opportunity was granted by order dated 07 th
September, 2026.
4. We are informed that upon terms of settlement being offered
by the borrowers, State Bank of India 5 has rejected the offer of A.
1  impugned order
2  W.P.(MD) Nos.23328, 21556, 22787 and 22789 of 2024
3  SARFAESI
4  MSMEs
5  SBI
2

--- Page 221 ---
Ganesamurthy, whereas, Canara Bank has rejected the offer of
Rajappa Rajkumar; however, the offer of S. Ashok Sundaresan is
under active consideration of the SBI.
5. Learned counsel appearing for the secured creditors, opposing
the submission advanced on behalf of the borrowers, have submitted
that no further opportunity ought to be given.
6. Having regard to the decisions of this Court in Pro Knits v.
Canara Bank6 as well as Shri Shri Swami Samarth Construction
& Finance Solution and Anr. v. Board of Directors of NKGSB
Co-Op. Bank Ltd. & Ors.7 delineating the rights and obligations of
MSMEs in default and upon consideration of the materials on record,
we are of the firm opinion that the borrowers did not set up any case
for interference and, hence, the impugned order of the High Court
cannot be sustained.
7. The impugned order is, accordingly, set aside.
8. The appeals are allowed on the following additional terms: -
(i) SBI may proceed to consider the offer of S. Ashok Sundaresan
in accordance with law and give its decision within a fortnight from
date.
(ii) Though the appeals are being allowed, as aforesaid, we grant
one last opportunity to A. Ganesamurthy and Rajappa Rajkumar to
submit proposals containing better terms of settlement within a week
from date; if such proposals are received, SBI and Canara Bank shall
dispose of the same in accordance with law.

"Report of the Sub-Committee constituted vide High Court

ARIJIT ROY @ ARAJIT ROY ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
THE STATE OF WEST BENGAL & ANR. ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal takes exception to the order dated 02.12.2025,
passed by the High Court at Calcutta (briefly the ‘High Court’
hereinafter) rejecting the prayer for anticipatory bail of the
appellant.
4. Appellant has been named as an accused in Arambagh Police
Station  Case  No.  255  of  2025,  registered  under  Sections
126(2)/117(2)/232(1)/76/352/351(2)/76  of  the  Bharatiya  Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023 (for short, ‘BNS’) subsequently Section 64 of BNS has
been added.
5. This Court by order dated 21.04.2026 had issued notice and
granted  interim  protection  to  the  appellant  subject  to  the
1

--- Page 234 ---
appellant cooperating with the investigation.
{
6. Learned counsel for the appellant has drawn the attention of
the  Court  to  the  initial  statement  of  the  de  facto
complainant/respondent  No.2  dated  04.05.2025  as  well  as  her
subsequent statement dated 19.06.2025 recorded before the Judicial
Magistrate. He submits that from a comparison of the two, it is
fairly evident that the allegation of outraging modesty etc. is an
afterthought.  Entire  case  has  political  overtones  because  of
appellant’s association with a particular political party. He
submits that pursuant to the interim protection granted to the
appellant, he has cooperated with the investigation and, therefore,
the interim protection may be made absolute.
{
7. On the other hand, learned State counsel has referred to the
counter affidavit filed on behalf of the State and submits that it
would be wrong to say that appellant has been implicated in the
case only because of political reasons. The allegations against the
appellant are quite serious. That apart, referring to paragraph 14
of the counter affidavit he submits that appellant has two criminal
antecedents of similar nature. In fact, one of them i.e., Arambagh
PS Case No.198 of 2026 was registered after the interim protection
was granted to the appellant by the Court. He therefore, submits
that the present may not be a fit case to grant anticipatory bail
to the appellant.
{
8. Supporting the submissions made on behalf of the State,
learned counsel appearing for the de  facto complainant/respondent
No.2 has drawn the attention of the Court to the counter affidavit
2

--- Page 235 ---
filed by her and submits that respondent No.2 was subjected to
physical and sexual abuse by the appellant which would be evident
from her statement made in the first information. She, therefore,
submits that the benefit of pre-arrest may not be extended to the
appellant.
9. In reply, learned counsel for the appellant submits that the
medical report placed on record would show that no such assault
etc. was suffered by the respondent No.2. Regarding the two
criminal antecedents he submits that these are also an outcome of
political rivalry. He submits that the way the complaints have been
registered display identical language and allegation against the
appellant.
{
10. We have considered the rival contentions made at the Bar and
have also perused the materials on record. On due consideration, we
are of the view that the interim protection granted to the
appellant may be made absolute subject to the appellant continuing
cooperating with the investigation and also furnishing undertaking
that  he  will  maintain  safe  distance  from  the  de  facto
complainant/respondent No.2 and shall not cause any harassment to
her in any manner whatsoever. Let the undertaking be furnished
before the concerned Investigating Officer within 15 (fifteen) days
from today.
11. Consequently,  impugned  order  of  the  High  Court  dated
02.12.2025 is set aside. Order dated 21.04.2026 is hereby made
absolute.
12. Appeal is accordingly allowed.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
1

--- Page 252 ---
2. Petitioner has been convicted under Section 302
of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’) by
the Additional Sessions Judge, Latur, Maharashtra in
Sessions Case No.46 of 2011 and sentenced to undergo
imprisonment for life.
3. Appeal  filed  by  the  petitioner  against  his
conviction and sentence was rejected by the High
Court of Judicature at Bombay, Bench at Aurangabad
(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), vide the
judgment  and  order  dated  21.08.2020  passed  in
Criminal Appeal No.539 of 2016.
4. On the basis of the imprisonment certificate
dated 03.02.2026, it can be seen that petitioner had
undergone  total  of  19  years  06  months  of
incarceration including the remission period. Minus
remission, he had undergone 13 years 11 months of
incarceration. In other words, as of now, petitioner
has completed more than 20 years of incarceration
including 14 years of actual incarceration.
5. On  27.07.2026,  we  had  issued  notice  on  the
Special Leave Petition as well as on the prayer for
permanent remission/bail.
6. This Court, in the case of In Re: Policy Strategy
for Grant of Bail [2025 SCC OnLine SC 349],  recorded
the following conclusions:
“21.  We,  therefore,  record  the  following
conclusions:
2

--- Page 253 ---
a) Where  there  is  a  policy  of  the
appropriate Government laying down guidelines
for consideration of the grant of premature
release under Section 432 of the CrPC or
Section 473 of the BNSS, it is the obligation
of the appropriate Government to consider
cases of all convicts for grant of premature
release as and when they become eligible for
consideration in terms of the policy. In such
a case, it is not necessary for the convict
or  his  relatives  to  make  a  specific
application for grant of permanent remission.
When  the  jail  manual  or  any  other
departmental  instruction  issued  by  the
appropriate Government contains such policy
guidelines,  the  aforesaid  direction  will
apply;
b) We  direct  those  States  and  Union
Territories that do not have a policy dealing
with the grant of remission in terms of
Section 432 of the CrPC or Section 473 of the
BNSS to formulate a policy within two months
from today;
c) Appropriate Government has the power to
incorporate suitable conditions in an order
granting permanent remission. Consideration
of various factors, which are mentioned in
paragraph 13 above by way of illustration, is
necessary before finalizing the conditions.
The conditions must aim at ensuring that the
criminal tendencies, if any, of the convict
remain  in  check  and  that  the  convict
rehabilitates himself in the society. The
conditions should not be so oppressive or
stringent that the convict is not able to
take  advantage  of  the  order  granting
permanent remission. The conditions cannot be
vague  and  should  be  capable  of  being
performed;
3

--- Page 254 ---
d) Order granting or refusing the relief of
permanent  remission  must  contain  brief
reasons. The order containing reasons should
be immediately communicated to the convict
through the office of the concerned prison.
The copies thereof should be forwarded to the
Secretaries of the concerned District Legal
Services Authorities. It is the duty of the
prison authorities to inform the convict that
he has the right to challenge the order of
rejection of the prayer for the grant of
remission.
e) As held in the case of Mafabhai Motibhai
Sagar, an order granting permanent remission
cannot  be  withdrawn  or  cancelled  without
giving an opportunity of being heard to the
convict.  An  order  of  cancellation  of
permanent  remission  must  contain  brief
reasons;
f) The District Legal Services Authorities
shall endeavour to implement NALSA SOP in its
true letter and spirit.
g) Further,  the  District  Legal  Services
Authorities shall also monitor implementation
of conclusion (a) as recorded above. For this
purpose,  the  District  Legal  Services
Authorities shall maintain the relevant date
of the convicts and as and when they become
eligible to a consideration for grant of
premature release, they shall do the needful
in terms of conclusion (a). The State Legal
Services  Authorities  shall  endeavour  to
create  a  portal  on  which  the  data  as
aforesaid  can  be  uploaded  on  real  time
basis.”
7. In terms of Paragraph 21(g) of the conclusions
extracted  herein  above,  District  Legal  Services
4

--- Page 255 ---
Authorities  have  been  mandated  to  monitor
implementation of conclusion (a). For this purpose,
the  District  Legal  Services  Authorities  shall
maintain the relevant date of the convicts and as and
when they become eligible for a consideration for
grant of premature release, they shall do the needful
in terms of conclusion (a). The State Legal Services
Authorities shall endeavour to create a portal on
which the data as aforesaid can be uploaded on real
time basis.
8. We, therefore, direct the appropriate Government,
i.e. State of Maharashtra, to consider the case for

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
Criminal Appeal No(s).  4388/2026
@ SLP (Crl) No. 4070/2026
KULSUM MIRZA @ MONA                                Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
NAHEED AFROZ KHAN & ORS.                           Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal is by the informant against the order of the
High Court dated 11.07.2025 passed in Criminal Petition No.
3631/2025. By the aforesaid order the High Court has quashed
the criminal proceedings against the first respondent.
4. The submission on behalf of the appellant is that there are
specific allegations in the First Information Report (for
short ‘FIR’) against the mother-in-law (first respondent
herein) and those allegations have been substantiated by the
materials collected during investigation, and also a charge-
sheet has been submitted indicting all accused including the
first respondent. However, for technical reasons it has not
1

--- Page 264 ---
been submitted against the third respondent, namely, the
father-in-law, as he had been absconding. It is submitted
that  the  High  Court  fell  in  error  in  quashing  the
proceedings against the first respondent by observing that
there are only bald and omnibus allegations against the
second accused, namely, the mother-in-law. It is submitted
that the said observation is incorrect because there are
specific allegations against the mother-in-law.
5. The  learned  counsel  representing  the  first  respondent
submits that a plain reading of the FIR would indicate that
several incidents of which allegations are there in the FIR
occurred outside the territory of India at Jeddah (Saudi
Arabia). Besides, there is material to indicate that no
complaint was made with the Consulate at Jeddah regarding
any atrocities on the informant either by her husband or
mother-in-law. In such circumstances, the order of the High
Court does not call for interference particularly when it is
a matter of common knowledge that in matters arising out of
matrimonial disputes, there is a tendency to rope in the
entire  family  of  the  husband.  Additionally,  no  useful
purpose would be served in continuing with the criminal
proceedings as by now parties are already divorced and are
now separately settled with their respective spouses. In
such circumstances, it is urged that it is not a fit case
2

--- Page 265 ---
where this Court should interfere with the order passed by
the High Court.
6. Having regard to the nature of the dispute, this Court vide
order dated 02.04.2026 referred the parties to mediation to
explore a settlement.
7. Despite mediation, no settlement could be arrived at between
the  parties.  The  Mediation  Centre  of  this  Court  has
reported, vide report dated 07.05.2026, that mediation could
not succeed. In such view of the matter, we would have to
consider whether the allegations made in the FIR and the
police report submitted after investigation make out a prima
facie case against the first respondent.
8. Insofar as the husband of the informant is concerned, his
petition was dismissed by the High Court upon finding that
the allegations do make out a prima facie case against him.
There is no challenge to the order of the High Court by the
husband of the informant and, therefore, we need not go into
the allegations made against him.
9. Insofar as the first respondent is concerned, a plain
reading of the FIR would indicate that there are allegations
against her of threatening, abusing and assaulting the
3

--- Page 266 ---
victim and even the dates of those incidents are mentioned
in the FIR. Besides, those allegations have prima facie been
supported  by  the  informant  and  other  witnesses  during
investigation in their statement(s) recorded under Section
161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
10. Having regard to the above, in our view, the High Court was
not  correct  in  holding  that  there  were  no  specific
allegations  against  the  first  respondent  and  whatever
allegations were there were general and omnibus in nature.
11. Consequently, this appeal is allowed. The impugned order to
the extent it quashes the criminal proceedings against the
first respondent is set aside. We, however, make it clear
that any observation in this order shall not prejudice the
Court while considering a discharge application of the first
respondent in case it is filed before the trial court.
                      
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
………………………………………….J
[MANOJ MISRA]
………………………………………….J
 [VIJAY BISHNOI]

1. Leave granted.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 4379     OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO. 12782/2026)
DILLIP KUMAR NAYAK               Appellant(s)
VERSUS
STATE OF ODISHA                              Respondent(s)
ORDER
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by order dated 19.05.2026
passed by the High Court of Orissa at Cuttack (briefly,
the  ‘High  Court’  hereinafter)  rejecting  the  bail
application of the appellant.
4. The appellant has been named as an accused in EOW PS
Case No. 13/2025 corresponding to C.T. Case No. 16/2025
pending  before  the  Designated  Court  at  Cuttack  and
registered under Sections  406/420/ 467/468/471 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, I.P.C.).
5. Briefly stated, the allegations against the appellant
is of using deceitful means to induce the informant and
his wife with the false assurance of providing profitable
returns for investment in the real estate business. In the
process, the appellant have duped the informant and his
wife for an amount of more than Rs. 12,00,00,000/- (Rupees
1    Crl. A. No. 4379 OF 2026

--- Page 270 ---
Twelve Crore) which amount was subsequently enhanced to
Rs.  15,00,00,000/-  (Rupees  Fifteen  Crore)  by
misappropriating the investment of the informant and his
wife  by  forging  documents  etc.  on  the  pretext  of
purchasing land for the real estate business in the name
of the informant and his wife. As a matter of fact, the
appellant had purchased the land in his own name, thus
defrauding the informant and his wife.
6. Appellant was arrested on 18.09.2025.
7. Mr. Rahul Kaushik, learned senior counsel for the
appellant  submits  that  investigation  is  complete,
whereafter  chargesheet  was  submitted  on  21.08.2026.
However, the trial has not yet commenced.  Appellant is in
custody for almost one year. Allegations levelled against
the appellant by the informant at best can constitute a
Civil claim. As a matter of fact, informant had already
instituted a Civil Suit for recovery of money.  In the
circumstances, he submits that appellant may be enlarged
on bail.  
8. Learned State Counsel on the other hand submits that
allegations against the appellant are quite serious.  He
had duped the informant and his wife for a huge sum of
money.  He further submits that appellant did not disclose
his criminal antecedents while seeking bail before the
High Court which was also taken note of by the High Court.
2    Crl. A. No. 4379 OF 2026

--- Page 271 ---
Therefore, at this stage, appellant may not be enlarged on
bail.
9. Mr.  Kaushik  Choudhary,  learned  counsel  for  the
informant  submits  that  the  criminal  intent  of  the
appellant is clearly manifest in the way he had duped the
informant  and  his  wife  of  their  hard  earned  money.
Referring to a recent decision of this Court in ‘ Rakesh
Mittal vs. Ajay Pal Gupta @Sonu Chaudhary and another’
(2026) INSC 161  decided on 17.02.2026, he submits that
benefit of bail may not be granted to a person who has
cheated innocent people like the informant and his wife of
their hard earned money.
10. We  have  given  our  anxious  consideration  to  the
submissions made at the Bar. We have noted that it is
almost  one  year  since  the  appellant  was  taken  into
custody.  The  charges  against  the  appellant  are  all
Magistrate-triable offences.  Investigation is complete
though the trial has not commenced. Prima facie, in such
circumstances, further detention of the appellant may not
be justified.
11. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned order of the
High Court dated 19.05.2026 and direct that the appellant
shall  be  produced  before  the  jurisdictional  Judicial
Magistrate within a maximum period of seven days from
today, whereafter he shall be released on bail on such
3    Crl. A. No. 4379 OF 2026

--- Page 272 ---
terms and conditions as may be deemed appropriate.
12.  Consequently, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
13.  Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

1. Leave granted.
2. The  appellants  have  approached  this  Court
challenging the impugned judgment dated 10.07.2019 passed
by the High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad in Letters Patent
Appeal No. 1412 Of 2018.
3. In the present case, a dispute arose in respect of
collection of parking fees/charges from the visitors as
well as members of the public by mall owners and owners of
the other properties in the township of Gujarat.
4. The  appellants  being  aggrieved  in  the  matter
approached the High Court of Gujarat and the learned Single
Judge passed an order allowing the writ petition.
1

--- Page 276 ---
5. Aggrieved  thereby,  a  Letters  Patent  Appeal/Writ
Appeal was preferred before the Division Bench of the High
Court whereby the Division Bench held that the mall owners
are not entitled to collect any parking fees/charges from
the visitors and rates were also fixed by the High Court in
respect of the parking fees/charges.
6. The matter was heard on a number of occasions, and
the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation as well as the State of
Gujarat were directed to frame a comprehensive parking
policy.
7. It has been brought to the notice of this Court that
a parking policy has since been framed for the city of
Ahmedabad, titled the  Parking Policy, 2021 , and parking
charges are now governed in terms thereof.
8. In light  of the  aforesaid development,  since a
comprehensive parking policy has already been framed by a
statutory body having expertise on the subject, the order
passed by the Division Bench of the High Court is set
aside. Nothing further survives for adjudication in the
present appeals.
9. The appellants shall strictly abide by the Parking
Policy, 2021 framed on the subject, as well as any other or
future parking policy that may be framed in the future by
the  Ahmedabad  Municipal  Corporation  or  by  the  State
2

--- Page 277 ---
Government.
10. The State/competent authority shall always be free
to provide and prescribe the rates and regulations for
parking of vehicles for persons visiting malls as well as
other public/commercial places.

applications  for  intervention,  stand  disposed  of
accordingly.

Leave granted.
This appeal challenges the judgment and order dated
17.04.2026 passed by the High Court of Jharkhand at Ranchi
in Bail Application No. 2825 of 2026.
The appellant herein has been booked for the crime
registered pursuant to FIR No.39/2025 dated 11.03.2025
lodged with Police Station Bokaro Steel City, District
Bokaro, with respect to offences punishable under Sections
317(2), 317(4), 317(5), 338, 336(3), 340(2) and 3(5) of
the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita,2023 (for short “BNS”).
An  application  seeking  regular  bail  having  been
rejected by the High Court  vide impugned order dated
17.04.2026,  the  appellant  has  preferred  the  instant
appeal.

--- Page 287 ---
2
By order dated 17-08-2026, the following order was
passed by this Court:
“Delay condoned. 
Issue notice to the respondent, returnable on 
31.08.2026.
Petitioner’s counsel is also permitted to serve 
the standing counsel for the respondent-State.”
Heard learned counsel for the appellant in support of
the appeal and learned counsel for the State and perused
the material on record. 
During the course of submissions, appellant’s counsel
drew our attention to order dated 13.02.2026 in SLP (Crl.)
No.19863/2025 in the case of Md. Prawej @ Md. Parwej vs.
State of Jharkhand arising out of a very same FIR. Learned
counsel for the appellant contended that on the principle
of parity, the relief of bail may be granted to the
appellant herein subject to the conditions to be imposed
by this Court. 
Per contra, learned counsel for the respondent-State
with reference to her reply contended that the aforesaid
order may not be followed in the instant case as the
appellant is the main culprit in this case from whom the
sixteen motor cycles were recovered and therefore any
relief of bail being granted to the appellant herein would
jeopardize the trial itself. She, therefore, submitted
that there is no merit in this appeal. 

--- Page 288 ---
3
We have considered the arguments advanced at the bar
and we find that in respect of similar allegations bail
was  granted  by  this  Court  vide  the  aforesaid  order.
Therefore following the principle of parity, we find that
the appellant ought to be extended a similar relief.
Considering the facts on record, in our view, the
case for bail is made out.
We, therefore, allow this appeal and direct as under:
“The appellant shall be produced before the
concerned Trial Court as early as possible and
the Trial Court shall release him on bail,
subject to such conditions as it may deem
appropriate to impose to ensure his presence
in  the  proceedings  arising  out  of  FIR
No.39/2025 dated 11.03.2025 mentioned above.”
It  is  directed  that  the  appellant  shall  extend
complete cooperation in the ensuing trial.
The appellant shall not misuse his liberty and shall
not in any way influence the witnesses or tamper with the
material on record.
Any  infraction  of  the  conditions  may  entail
cancellation of bail granted to the appellant.

--- Page 289 ---
4
With the aforesaid directions, the Criminal Appeal is
allowed.

2026, registered under Sections 120-B/420/467/468 and 471 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’).
5. Allegation against the appellant is that appellant and his
associates, including his brother and nephew, had deceived the
informant pretending to be a friend and persuading the informant to
believe that an auction of Jagannath Prasad Balighat was held.
Informant was impressed upon that since the appellant did not have
much solvency to take the sand  mahal on lease, he should provide
for a sum of  60,00,000₹ /- (Rupees Sixty Lakhs Only) for which

1

--- Page 297 ---
regard.  According  to  the  informant,  the  appellant  earned

but did not pay back to the informant. It is on such allegations
that the related police case came to be registered.
6. This Court by order dated 29.06.2026 had issued notice and
granted  interim  protection  to  the  appellant  subject  to  the
appellant cooperating with the investigation.
7. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that the allegations
made against the appellant pertains to a dispute of civil nature
relating to sharing of profits. He has extensively referred to the

2

--- Page 298 ---

interim protection granted to the appellant may be made absolute.

02.05.2026 and make our order dated 29.06.2026 absolute.

BUDHU BHUTIYA                 APPELLANT(S)

ORDER
1.   Leave granted.
2. We  have  heard  Mr.  Ratnakar  Dash,  learned  Senior
counsel for the appellant and Mr. Vinayak Sharma , learned
counsel for the respondent-State of Chattisgarh.
3. In  this  appeal,  the  appellant  has  assailed  the
legality and correctness of the order dated 14.05.2026
passed  by  the  High  Court  of  Chattisgarh  at  Bilaspur
(briefly, the ‘High Court’ hereinafter) rejecting the bail
prayer of the appellant.
4. The allegations against the appellant is that acting
on the basis of specific information , police of Si nghoda
Police Station intercepted two vehicles, on search thereof,
five plastic bags containing  ganja were recovered.  On
being weighed, the total quantity of the contraband was
found to be 137 kilograms.  The persons in the two
1            Crl. A. @SLP (Crl.) No.  13607/2026

--- Page 312 ---
vehicles, Dilshad Khan and Sheikh Jabbar  were apprehended.
Based on their confessional statements, co-accused Narottam
Behera, Shiv Sahu and Sushil Kumar Sahu were arrested.  On
the basis of the further confessional statements of the
aforesaid co-accused, appellant came to be apprehended on
24.02.2026.  Since then, he has been in custody.
5. On 03.08.2026, this Court had issued notice.
6. Learned senior counsel for the appellant submits that
appellant was not present at the spot when the contraband
was seized, neither in the vehicles nor in the immediate
vicinity.  He came to be implicated on the basis of the
confessional statements made by the co-accused which is per
se not admissible. No recovery was made from the appellant.
The appellant has been in custody for almost seven months
now. Investigation is complete whereafter charge-sheet has
been filed. Therefore, further detention of the appellant
may not be necessary.
7. Per  contra ,  learned  State  counsel  submits  that
appellant is the mastermind behind the entire operation.
Referring to the counter affidavit filed on behalf of the
State,  he  submits  that  during  the  course  of  the
investigation, Call Detail Records (CDR) of the accused
persons were collected and analysed.  On the basis of the
analysis of the CDR, it is evident that all the accused
persons including the appellant were in constant touch with
each other. The appellant is very much involved in the
2            Crl. A. @SLP (Crl.) No.  13607/2026

--- Page 313 ---
offence.  Additionally, he submits that appellant is a
resident of Orissa. Therefore, procuring his present during
the trial would be an issue that may be taken into
consideration by the Court.
8. We have duly considered the submissions made and have
also perused the materials on record.  We find that in all
there  are  eight accused  persons.  Total  quantity  of
contraband seized is 137 kilograms. As of now, there is no
apportionment  of  the  contraband  between  the  accused
persons.  This is relevant because the commercial quantity
of ganja is twenty kilograms or more.  We further find that
the co-accused have already been enlarged on bail by the
Court.  Investigation is complete whereafter charge-sheet
has been filed though the charges have not yet been framed.
9. In such circumstances, we are inclined to grant bail
to the appellant.  Consequently, we set aside the impugned
order of the High Court dated 14.05.2026 and direct that
the appellant shall be produced before the jurisdictional
Special Court within a maximum period of seven days from
today whereafter he shall be enlarged on bail on such terms
and conditions as may be deemed appropriate.
10. We further direct that the appellant shall appear on
each and every date of hearing before the Trial Court
except on such occasions when his presence be exempted by
the Trial Court.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

SANTOSH KUMAR ..... APPELLANT(S)

VINOD KUMAR N.S. & ANR. ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The grievance of the appellant, Santosh Kumar, falls within a
short compass.  In his application filed before the High
Court  of  Kerala  seeking  suspension  of  sentence,  viz.,
Criminal M.A. No. 1/2026 in Criminal Revision Petition No.
17/2026, the appellant specifically cited the grounds as to
why he should not be mulcted with the requirement of paying
the fine amount or a part thereof as a condition precedent
for grant of relief.  Paragraphs 4 and 5 in the said
application related to this aspect and read as under: - 
“4. The  petitioner  is  under  extreme  financial
stress and economic hardship.  He is living in
rented house along with his mother, wife and two
children.
5. The petitioner has no employment and financial
capacity to deposit any amount with his minimal
1

--- Page 317 ---
Crl.A. @ SLP(Crl.) No. 6307/2026
source of income that may be ordered and hence
sentence  may  be  suspended  without  imposing
condition for payment.”
3. However, we find from the impugned order dated 27.02.2026,
that the High Court did not even consider the aforestated
grounds cited by the appellant and straightaway directed
deposit of 40% of the fine amount as one of the conditions
for  granting  suspension  of  sentence  and  bail  to  the
appellant.
4. This non-application of mind by the High Court cannot be
countenanced in the light of the law laid down by this Court
in  Jamboo  Bhandari  vs.  Madhya  Pradesh  State  Industrial
Development Corporation Ltd. & Ors. 1. We are, thus, left with
no  option  but  to  set  aside  the  impugned  order  dated
27.02.2026 on this short ground.
5. The appeal is accordingly allowed, setting aside the impugned
order dated 27.02.2026.  The application, viz., Criminal M.A.
No. 1/2026 filed by the appellant in Criminal Revision
Petition No. 17/2026 shall stand restored on the file of the
High  Court  for  consideration  afresh.  Pending  such
consideration, the appellant, Santosh Kumar, shall not be
arrested for serving the sentence imposed upon him.
6. We request the High Court to dispose of Criminal M.A. No.
1/2026 as expeditiously as possible.  The same shall be
considered on its own merits and in accordance with law.

                             O R D E R
1. Our order dated 05th March, 2025 speaks for itself. The
order reads thus:-
“1. The petitioner – herein is a registered charitable
1

--- Page 336 ---
trust. 
2.  Some  time  in  1980,  the  Respondent  No.1,  an
instrumentality  of  State,  within  Article  12  of  the
Constitution allotted 14 acres of land in favour of the
Trust by way of a lease deed initially for a period of 30
years keeping the options open for further renewal.
3. The petitioner – Trust set up a School on the leased
land. The first 30 years of the lease period came to an
end on 6-4-2010.
4. We are informed that an amount of Rs.900/- and odd was
being paid towards the lease rental by the school to the
Respondent No.1. After the lease period came to an end on
6-4-2010, the petitioner – Trust requested the Respondent
No.1 to renew the lease further. However, the same was
declined. This triggered the dispute between the parties.
5. Initially, the petitioner invoked writ jurisdiction of
the High Court and later in point of time, instituted a
suit seeking various reliefs.
6. The suit came to be dismissed. The first appeal
preferred by the petitioner also came to be dismissed.
7.  In  such  circumstances,  referred  to  above,  the
petitioner - Trust is here before us with the present
petition.
8. In the plaint, the following reliefs were prayed
for :-
“1. That the injunction be granted in favour of
the plaintiff and against the defendant thereby
permanently  restraining  the  defendants  from
dispossessing the plaintiff from the disputed land
and the letter issued by the defendants bearing
no. Estt/Land/E-14/2015 dated 26.6.2015 and letter
no.  Estt/Land/E-14/2013/22  dated  4.4.2013  be
annulled. Further, the defendant be restrained
from interfering with the peaceful possession of
the plaintiff.
2. That the defendants be directed to renew the
lease in favour of the plaintiff in terms of the
conditions of the lease executed on 7.4.1980.
3.  That  the  defendants  be  directed  to  pay
2

--- Page 337 ---
litigation charges to the plaintiff.
4. Any other order that the Hon'ble Court deems
fit in the facts and circumstances of the case.”
9. If we go strictly by law, then probably the petitioner
– Trust may not have any case on merits. However, we
should  be  mindful  of  the  fact  that  there  are  1700
students studying in this School as on date.
10. We believe that the dispute can be resolved. The
petitioner – Trust does not require 14 acres of land to
run the School.
11. The Respondent No.1 should consider allowing the
trust to retain the portion of land on which the school
is standing as on date along with some sizeable area for
the purpose of a play ground.
12. The aforesaid can be worked out mutually.
13. The rest of the land can be taken over by Respondent
No.1. Besides the same, the parties can also talk as
regards the lease rental to be paid either per month or
per annum.
14. The learned counsel appearing for the Respondent No.1
was gracious enough to receive what has fallen from this
Court. He would like to speak to his client and get back.
15. Post this matter after four weeks.
16. During the interregnum period, we would like the
parties to meet and talk as regards what has fallen from
this Court and recorded in this order.”
2. It has been more than 1½ years since the time we
passed the order referred to above. It seems that there has
been no further headway in the matter.
3. We are informed that the Trust is running a School. As
on date, there are more than 1700 students studying in the
School and most of them are tribals.
4. The  parties  before  us,  i.e.,  the  Trust  and  the
3

--- Page 338 ---
respondent no.1 may be in talks with each other for some
amicable  settlement,  however,  we  want  the  District
